sentences.text: Simone's aunt Rosa lived in a village called Ceglie in the far south of Italy, in the heel of the boot, in the region called Puglia.
It was a small hilltop village of whitewashed stone houses packed close together, surrounded by dry olive groves and rocky pastures.
Nothing much happened there.
In summer the sun was very strong.
The people were mostly very old.
Most of the young ones had moved away to the cities.
Aunt Rosa was fifty-three and she was not old, but she had chosen to stay.
She had a small yard where she grew tomatoes and basil, and she made her own cheese from her two goats, and she was, Simone thought, the happiest person he knew.
Simone was eleven and lived the rest of the year in Milan, which was as far from Puglia as you could get in Italy without leaving the country.
He had come to spend all of August with Aunt Rosa.
His parents had gone on a trip.
He was here alone.
He had been here for many summers before.
He knew everyone in Ceglie.
Everyone knew him.
Whenever he walked through the little square, the old men playing cards outside the café would call his name and wave.
Aunt Rosa's house was in the middle of a row of three small houses, all identical, all whitewashed, all with old wooden doors and one small window each.
On one side of Aunt Rosa lived Signor Bruno, who was eighty-one, and on the other side lived Signor Marco, who was seventy-eight.
They were brothers.
They looked alike, though Bruno was thinner.
They were both widowers.
They both lived alone.
They both had lived in their houses for their entire lives — their parents had lived in the same houses before them, and their grandparents before that.
They saw each other every day.
They lived less than five meters apart.
And they had not spoken to each other in forty-three years.
Simone knew this because everyone in Ceglie knew this.
It was a small village and this was the biggest strange thing in it.
Signor Bruno went to the café at three in the afternoon and drank his coffee at the table on the left.
Signor Marco went to the café at three in the afternoon and drank his coffee at the table on the right.
They never looked at each other.
They never spoke.
They shopped at the same grocery on different days.
They went to the same church on different Sundays.
It had been like this since 1982, when they had had — nobody in the village was sure what — some kind of terrible fight.
Nobody remembered what the fight had been about.
Bruno and Marco remembered.
But neither of them had told anyone.
Neither of them had explained.
They had simply stopped speaking, and they had never started again.
Simone had noticed this for years.
He had asked his aunt about it many times.
Aunt Rosa always said the same thing: "It is very sad.
But it is between them.
It is not for us to fix." And Simone had accepted this.
He had said hello to Signor Bruno when he came out to sit on his step.
He had said hello to Signor Marco when he came out to sit on his step.
He had not tried to do anything about the situation, because he had understood, from Aunt Rosa, that it was not his place.
And he had been small.
And what could a small boy have done anyway.
On the second day of Simone's visit, in the afternoon, Signor Bruno called out to him as he was walking past.
"Simone.
Come here for a moment." Simone went over.
Signor Bruno was sitting on his front step with a small folded piece of paper in his hand.
He looked embarrassed.
He said, quietly, "Simone.
Can you do a favor for me.
A very small favor.
Nobody has to know.
Just — take this piece of paper.
Knock on Marco's door.
Give it to him.
Say nothing.
Do you understand?"
Simone looked at the paper.
He looked at Signor Bruno.
He was ten different kinds of surprised.
He said, "Signor Bruno — I — yes.
Yes, of course." Signor Bruno handed him the paper.
His hand shook a little.
Simone took it.
He walked past his aunt's door, and he stopped at Signor Marco's door, and he knocked.
His heart was beating in his ears.
Signor Marco opened the door.
He was surprised to see Simone.
He said, "Simone.
What is it.
Is your aunt okay." Simone said, "Yes.
She is fine." He held out the paper.
"Signor Bruno asked me to give you this." Signor Marco went very still.
He looked at the paper.
He looked at Simone.
He looked at the paper again.
He did not take it.
He was quiet for a long moment.
Then he said, in a very careful voice, "Bruno asked you." "Yes," said Simone.
"He said to give it to you and not to say anything else." Signor Marco slowly reached out.
He took the paper.
He looked at it in his hand.
He did not open it.
He said, "Thank you, Simone.
That is all." And he closed the door.
Simone stood in the alley for a moment.
Then he walked back past his aunt's door.
Signor Bruno was still sitting on his front step.
He looked up.
Simone said, "He took it.
He did not open it.
Not while I was there." Signor Bruno nodded.
He said, "Thank you, Simone.
Do not tell your aunt." Simone said, "Okay." And he went inside.
